summary: Smit et al. provide the corpus's primary null-result evidence on multi-agent debate (MAD): MAD systems in their current form do not reliably outperform self-consistency or ensembling (Smit C001; PDF PAGE 1), and Medprompt (non-debate) performs best overall across the seven evaluated datasets (Smit C003; Table 2, PDF PAGE 5). The null is qualified: on medical datasets every system except Multi-Persona beats single-agent, whereas on non-medical reasoning datasets single-agent surpasses most MAD systems (Smit C005; PDF PAGE 5). Smit also attribute the gap to hyperparameter sensitivity — agreement intensity can reverse rankings, with tuned Multi-Persona surpassing Medprompt and Self-Consistency (~15% gain on USMLE) — and they document API-variability and cost limitations (Smit C006–C008; PDF PAGES 1, 6, 9). Zhang et al. supply the boundary conditions: across 36 configurations (4 models × 9 benchmarks) no MAD method exceeds a 20% win rate over CoT, and adjusting agents/rounds does not reverse the result (Zhang C001–C002; PDF PAGES 1, 3). Task type matters: MAD performs worse on programming (only SoM/AgentVerse positive) but better on mathematical reasoning (Zhang C003; PDF PAGE 7). MAD also converts tokens less efficiently than Self-Consistency (Zhang C005; PDF PAGE 9), and model heterogeneity (Heter-MAD) consistently improves all tested MAD frameworks, with gains attributed to solving CW/WC questions (Zhang C006; PDF PAGES 11–12). These results directly conflict with Du et al.'s reported debate gains, which we reconcile through three design inferences below.
unresolved: Whether Smit's K-fold medical/non-medical split generalizes beyond their seven datasets.
Whether Zhang et al.'s null results extend to more complex reasoning tasks beyond the nine benchmarks.
The exact token/latency accounting rules for the evaluation plan (e.g., whether to count debate rounds) are not fully specified and must be fixed by the parent.
